segments.text: The format for running the [[p0]] command is:
In the simplest case, two file names [[p0]] and [[p1]] are given, and [[p2]] compares the contents of [[p3]] and [[p4]]. A file name of [[p5]] stands for the standard input.
If one file is a directory and the other is not, [[p0]] compares the file in the directory whose name is that of the non-directory. The non-directory file must not be [[p1]].

If two file names are given and both are directories, [[p0]] compares corresponding files in both directories, in alphabetical order; this comparison is not recursive unless the [[p1]] ([[p2]]) option is given. [[p3]] never compares the actual contents of a directory as if it were a file. The file that is fully specified may not be standard input, because standard input is nameless and the notion of “file with the same name” does not apply.
If the [[p0]] option is given, the number of file names is arbitrary, and [[p1]] is compared to each named file. Similarly, if the [[p2]] option is given, each named file is compared to [[p3]].

[[p0]] options begin with ‘[[p1]]’, so normally file names may not begin with ‘[[p2]]’. However, [[p3]] as an argument by itself treats the remaining arguments as file names even if they begin with ‘[[p4]]’.
An exit status of 0 means no differences were found, 1 means some differences were found, and 2 means trouble.

Below is a summary of all of the options that GNU [[p0]] accepts. Most options have two equivalent names, one of which is a single letter preceded by ‘[[p1]]’, and the other of which is a long name preceded by ‘[[p2]]’. Multiple single letter options (unless they take an argument) can be combined into a single command line word: [[p3]] is equivalent to [[p4]]. Long named options can be abbreviated to any unique prefix of their name. Brackets ([ and ]) indicate that an option takes an optional argument.
